agent_trace.summary: On abdominal CT, abnormality description questions usually focus on identifying gross structural changes in the bowel, mesentery, retroperitoneum, abdominal wall, or solid organs. The retrieved similar cases show that CT findings may involve either an organ-based mass (e.g., kidney) or a bowel complication such as obstruction/perforation, so attention to bowel caliber, free air, fluid, and surrounding fat is important.

key_facts: Normal bowel loops should have expected caliber without marked dilation or collapse.
Mesenteric fat should not show significant stranding, edema, or focal soft-tissue infiltration.
Retroperitoneal structures such as the psoas muscles, vessels, and lumbar vertebral body should have preserved contour and no adjacent inflammatory change.
Free intraperitoneal air, extraluminal contrast, or focal fluid collections can suggest perforation or other acute pathology.
Abdominal wall defects, hernias, masses, or fluid collections may also be visible on CT.
